newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch aim to seal EMU entry with 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Dutch aim to seal EMU entry with 1997 budget.

text.p: The Dutch government unveiled a 1997 budget on Tuesday aimed at confirming the country's status as a frontrunner for economic and monetary union (EMU) in the crucial qualifying year for the single currency project.
European Union countries' eligibility for full monetary union will be judged on the basis of their performance next year on a series of so-called convergence criteria.
But Dutch politicians and officials, right up to the highest level, are already convinced their country will make the grade.

"It can be confidently predicted that the Netherlands will be eligible to participate in EMU as soon as it commences in 1999," Queen Beatrix said in her traditional budget-day speech outlining government policy for the new parliamentary year.

Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm said a combination of economic growth and prudent financial management had put the ruling tripartite coalition of left and right-wing parties well on track to achieving all of its policy goals.

"Whether you look at employment, economic growth, the deficit, national debt, tax and premium relief or purchasing power, it is all developing in line with, or better than, envisaged in the 1994 coalition accord," Zalm said.
"We are not there yet, but the trend is encouraging," he told a pre-budget news briefing.
Government economists see real growth of gross domestic product (GDP) picking up to 2.75 percent in 1997 from 2.5 percent in 1996, outpacing the European Union (EU) average.
Inflation is seen edging up to 2.5 percent from 2.25 percent but will still be low enough to qualify for EMU.
The public sector deficit is projected to fall to 2.2 percent of GDP from 2.6 percent, well below the three percent required for EMU entry.

The deficit will be Zalm's calling card in Brussels, for total public sector debt, at 76.2 percent of GDP, will still be well above the 60 percent EMU norm, despite a hefty reduction of 2.6 percentage points compared with 1996.

Zalm said roughly 60 percent of the fall in the debt ratio was attributable to budget discipline and economic growth while the remaining 40 percent reflected a one-off financial windfall. This stems from drawing down an obsolete government cash reserve held at the Dutch central bank.
Subsequent budgets would bring further reductions in both the deficit and public debt, he added.
Budget documents show that unemployment, which started to fall in 1995, is expected to decline further this year and next, as job growth outstrips growth of the labour force.

The government's Central Planning Bureau (CPB) predicts that over 100,000 new jobs will be created in both 1996 and 1997, while the number of new job seekers coming onto the labour market is estimated at some 70,000 a year.
As a result the government expects to achieve its target of creating 350,000 new jobs during its four-year term of office one year ahead of schedule in 1997.
Unemployment is expected to fall to 5.25 percent of the labour force from 6.0 percent in 1996.
Falling jobless totals have recently helped to bring down the number of people of working age who receive welfare benefits after a relentless rise since the 1970s.
Overall labour market participation has gradually risen too, with the proportion of non-workers in the 15-65 age group set to fall to 78.3 per 100 workers from 81.6 per 100 workers in 1995.
